problem: If $3p+4q=8$ and $4p+3q=13$, what is $q$ equal to?

response.problem_brief: Find q given the linear system 3p+4q=8 and 4p+3q=13.

approaches.name: Classical Elimination
approaches.core_idea: Eliminate one variable by forming a linear combination of the two equations so that one coefficient cancels, then solve for the remaining variable, and back-substitute if desired.
plan: Multiply one or both equations by suitable constants so that the coefficients of p (or q) become equal and opposite.
Add or subtract the modified equations to eliminate p (or q).
Solve the resulting single-variable linear equation to find q (if p was eliminated).
Optionally back-substitute into one original equation to check consistency.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses linear combinations of whole equations to cancel a variable directly.

approaches.name: Substitution Method
approaches.core_idea: Explicitly solve one equation for one variable in terms of the other, then substitute into the second to obtain an equation in a single variable, which can be solved for q.
plan: Rearrange one of the equations, e.g., 3p+4q=8, to express p in terms of q.
Substitute this expression for p into the second equation 4p+3q=13.
Simplify the resulting equation to a single-variable linear equation in q.
Solve for q and, if desired, plug back to find p for a check.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: First isolates a variable algebraically, then substitutes, instead of combining equations to cancel.

approaches.name: Matrix / Inverse of 2×2 System
approaches.core_idea: View the system as a 2×2 matrix equation and solve using the inverse matrix formula or Cramer’s rule; extract q from the resulting vector solution.
plan: Write the system in matrix form A·[p q]^T = b with A = [[3,4],[4,3]] and b = [8,13]^T.
Compute det(A) and form A^{-1} using the standard 2×2 inverse formula, or set up Cramer’s rule for q.
Apply A^{-1}·b to get [p q]^T, or compute the determinant ratio for q via Cramer’s rule.
Simplify to obtain the numeric value of q.
Optionally verify by substituting into the original equations.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Treats the system as a matrix equation and uses determinant/inverse machinery rather than ad hoc elimination.

approaches.name: Add-and-Subtract Symmetric Combination
approaches.core_idea: Exploit symmetry by adding and subtracting the equations to get equations in (p+q) and (p−q), solve those, then recover q from p+q and p−q.
plan: Add the two equations to obtain an equation involving (p+q).
Subtract one equation from the other to obtain an equation involving (p−q).
Solve the resulting two simple linear equations for p+q and p−q.
Use (p+q) and (p−q) to solve for p and q individually (e.g., via averaging and half-difference).

problem: Let $f(x) = Ax + B$ and $g(x) = Bx + A$, where $A \neq B$. If $f(g(x)) - g(f(x)) = B - A$, what is $A + B$?

response.problem_brief: Find A + B given linear functions f(x)=Ax+B and g(x)=Bx+A, with A≠B and the condition f(g(x))−g(f(x))=B−A for all x.

approaches.name: Direct Expansion and Polynomial Identity
approaches.core_idea: Explicitly compose the linear functions, simplify both compositions to polynomials in x, subtract, and equate coefficients with the constant expression B−A. Use the fact that the identity must hold for all x to get equations in A and B, then solve for A+B.
plan: Compute g(x)=Bx+A and then f(g(x))=A(Bx+A)+B
Compute f(x)=Ax+B and then g(f(x))=B(Ax+B)+A
Simplify each composition into standard linear form in x
Form f(g(x))−g(f(x)) and simplify to a polynomial in x
Use that this polynomial must equal the constant B−A for all x, so equate the coefficient of x to 0 and the constant term to B−A
Solve the resulting system for A and B
Compute A+B from the found values
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses full polynomial expansion and coefficient comparison from an identity in x.

approaches.name: Evaluate at Two Convenient x-Values
approaches.core_idea: Use that f(g(x))−g(f(x)) is given to be the constant B−A for all x, so its value at any x is B−A. Pick two convenient values of x (e.g., x=0 and x=1) to get two separate equations in A and B and solve for A+B.
plan: Compute general expressions for f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) (at least in a partially simplified form)
Evaluate f(g(x))−g(f(x)) at x=0 and set it equal to B−A
Evaluate f(g(x))−g(f(x)) at x=1 and set it equal to B−A
Simplify the two resulting equations to relations between A and B
Solve this small system for A and B (or directly for A+B)
Conclude the value of A+B from these relations
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Avoids full coefficient comparison by using the constancy of the expression and plugging in specific x-values.

approaches.name: Matrix Representation of Linear Functions
approaches.core_idea: Represent each linear function as a 2×2 matrix acting on column vectors [x;1], then composition corresponds to matrix multiplication. Compute the matrices for f∘g and g∘f, subtract, and enforce that the resulting affine transformation equals the constant map B−A to derive equations for A and B.
plan: Represent f(x)=Ax+B as matrix F=[[A,B],[0,1]] and g(x)=Bx+A as G=[[B,A],[0,1]] on vectors [x;1]
Compute the product matrices FG and GF to represent f∘g and g∘f
Compute FG−GF and interpret the resulting matrix as the affine transformation corresponding to f(g(x))−g(f(x))
Translate the condition f(g(x))−g(f(x))=B−A into conditions on entries of FG−GF (coefficient of x must be 0, constant term must be B−A)
Equate the appropriate matrix entries to obtain equations in A and B
Solve these equations to find A and B, then compute A+B
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Recasts the problem as matrix multiplication and commutator comparison of 2×2 affine matrices.

approaches.name: Symmetry via Swapping A and B
approaches.core_idea: Observe that swapping A and B interchanges f and g and changes the sign of B−A, imposing an antisymmetry. Use this symmetry plus one expansion or evaluation to constrain A and B more quickly, then solve for A+B.
plan: Note that under swapping A↔B, f and g are exchanged and B−A becomes A−B (sign flip)
Compute f(g(x))−g(f(x)) in general and recognize its structure is antisymmetric in A and B
Use the antisymmetry to infer that the expression must factor through (A−B), simplifying the form of f(g(x))−g(f(x))
Equate this factored form to B−A, which is −(A−B), to deduce a simple relation between A and B
Resolve this relation (possibly using one specific x-value) to find concrete values (or relation) for A and B
Compute A+B from the deduced values
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Exploits the A↔B interchange symmetry to infer a factorization in (A−B) before solving constraints.

EXPLANATION:
The problem is not so simple as to force a single standard method; different mathematical viewpoints are plausible.

- **Approach 1** and **Approach 2** both:
  - Explicitly compute \(f(g(x))\) and \(g(f(x))\) as algebraic expressions in \(x\).
  - Use the fact that the identity \(f(g(x)) - g(f(x)) = B - A\) holds for all \(x\).
  - Derive equations in \(A\) and \(B\) from these expressions and solve them.
  
  The only difference is *how* they exploit the “for all \(x\)” condition (coefficient comparison vs plugging in two values), but both are the same core algebraic/function-equation mechanism on polynomials in \(x\). They form a single approach class.

- **Approach 3** uses a **linear algebra / matrix representation** of affine maps:
  - Represents \(f\) and \(g\) as \(2\times 2\) matrices.
  - Uses matrix multiplication to represent composition and then interprets matrix entries.
  
  This is a different structural viewpoint (affine transformations via matrices), so it is a distinct approach.

- **Approach 4** is based on **symmetry/antisymmetry in \(A\) and \(B\)**:
  - Analyzes the effect of swapping \(A\) and \(B\) on \(f,g\), and on the right-hand side \(B-A\).
  - Uses antisymmetry to infer factorization and relations in \(A\) and \(B\).
  
  This relies on a symmetry argument rather than straightforward expansion or matrix composition, so it is also a distinct approach.

Thus we have three mechanism-level approaches: algebraic composition (1 & 2), matrix/linear-algebraic (3), and symmetry-based (4).

problem: Define a $\it{good\ word}$ as a sequence of letters that consists only of the letters $A$, $B$, and $C$ --- some of these letters may not appear in the sequence --- and in which $A$ is never immediately followed by $B$, $B$ is never immediately followed by $C$, and $C$ is never immediately followed by $A$. How many seven-letter good words are there?

response.problem_brief: Count the number of length-7 words over {A,B,C} where AB, BC, and CA never appear as adjacent pairs.

approaches.name: State Automaton + Recurrence
approaches.core_idea: View the word as a walk on a directed graph whose vertices are the letters {A,B,C} and allowed edges are the permitted adjacencies. Set up recurrences for the number of valid words ending in each letter and iterate them up to length 7.
plan: Draw the directed graph on vertices A,B,C with edges corresponding to allowed consecutive letters (exclude AB, BC, CA).
Let a_n, b_n, c_n be the numbers of good words of length n ending in A,B,C respectively.
Write recurrence relations for a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}, c_{n+1} in terms of a_n, b_n, c_n using the allowed edges of the graph.
Determine initial conditions for n=1 (each of A,B,C is allowed as the first letter).
Compute (a_n, b_n, c_n) step-by-step up to n=7 using the recurrence.
Sum a_7 + b_7 + c_7 to get the total number of good 7-letter words.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses a 3-state directed graph and direct recurrence iteration, without matrix or eigenvalue machinery.

approaches.name: Adjacency Matrix Exponentiation (By Hand)
approaches.core_idea: Model transitions between letters with a 3×3 adjacency matrix whose (i,j) entry is 1 if j may follow i. The number of length-7 words is expressed via powers of this matrix, computed by repeated squaring or iteration by hand.
plan: Form the 3×3 adjacency matrix M where rows/columns correspond to A,B,C and M_{ij}=1 if j can follow i, 0 otherwise, respecting the forbidden pairs AB, BC, CA.
Recognize that the number of length-n words corresponds to sums of entries of M^{n-1}, possibly with an initial all-ones vector (for starting letters).
Compute successive powers M^2, M^3, …, M^{6} by hand, looking for simplifications or patterns (e.g., symmetry, repeated rows).
At each step, track how row sums evolve, or track multiplication of an initial vector (1,1,1) by M^{n-1}.
Once M^{6} or (1,1,1)·M^{6} is obtained, sum appropriate entries to get the total count for length-7 words.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Treats the problem as counting walks via matrix powers, rather than scalar recurrences per terminal letter.

approaches.name: Pattern Decomposition by Adjacent Equal/Different Letters
approaches.core_idea: Classify good words by the positions where letters change versus stay the same. Use the combinatorics of allowed changes (which are directionally restricted) to count possibilities by structure of change runs.
plan: Describe any word by a pattern of length 6 indicating, for each adjacent pair, whether the next letter is the same (S) or different (D).

Analyze the restriction on D steps: when a change occurs, the direction A→C is allowed but not A→B; B→A allowed but not B→C; C→B allowed but not C→A. This gives exactly one allowed new letter for each change given the previous letter.
Note that for S steps, the next letter is forced to be the same as the previous one.

For a fixed S/D pattern, count how many words realize it: choose the initial letter (3 choices), then each S step forces no change, and each D step forces the unique allowed change, so all internal choices are forced.
Conclude that each S/D pattern yields exactly 3 good words; determine how many S/D patterns are possible (all 2^6 since there is no further restriction at the pattern level).
Multiply the number of S/D patterns by 3 to obtain the total count of 7-letter good words.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Counts via binary patterns of ‘same vs. different’ adjacent positions, exploiting that each change has exactly one legal target letter.

approaches.name: Encoding as Directed Cycle Orientation and Using Symmetry
approaches.core_idea: Interpret {A,B,C} arranged on a directed 3-cycle (A→B→C→A) where forbidden adjacencies follow the cycle direction, and allowed changes go opposite or stay. Use this symmetric picture to derive a compact recurrence for counts of sequences by net number of direction-reversing steps.
plan: Place letters on a directed 3-cycle A→B→C→A so that forbidden pairs follow the arrow; allowed changes correspond to either staying put or moving against the arrow.
Associate each sequence with a path on this 3-cycle where each step is either ‘stay’ or ‘move against the arrow’.
Note that regardless of the current vertex, an ‘against-arrow’ move is always uniquely determined, giving a fixed pattern of movement on the 3-cycle.

Let f_n be the total number of good words of length n; derive a scalar recurrence for f_n by considering extension by ‘stay’ vs. ‘move’ steps in terms of previous positions and using the 3-fold symmetry of the cycle.
Solve or iterate this scalar recurrence up to n=7 to obtain f_7 directly, without tracking separate counts for A,B,C.
Conclude with f_7 as the number of 7-letter good words.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Leverages rotational symmetry of the letters on a directed 3-cycle to collapse the system into a single scalar recurrence in total counts.

judge_result:
EXPLANATION:
The problem is not “simple” in the sense of the simplicity rule; there are several natural ways to model the adjacency restrictions, so multiple distinct approaches are meaningful.

- **Approach 1 (State Automaton + Recurrence)**: Models words as walks on a directed graph with states A,B,C, and derives a system of recurrences for counts ending in each letter. This is a classic state-based/dynamic-programming treatment on a finite automaton.

- **Approach 2 (Adjacency Matrix Exponentiation)**: Encodes the same transition structure in a 3×3 matrix and uses matrix powers to count length‑7 walks. This explicitly uses linear algebra / matrix viewpoint rather than scalar recurrences in components. Even though it is algebraically related to Approach 1, the core mechanism is “matrix exponentiation” as opposed to “component-wise recurrence.”

- **Approach 3 (Pattern Decomposition by S/D)**: Re-encodes each word by a binary pattern (Same vs Different) between adjacent letters, then uses the fact that given any S/D pattern and initial letter, all letters are forced. Counting reduces to counting binary strings of length 6 and multiplying by 3. This is a combinatorial pattern-encoding approach, not a state-graph/recurrence or matrix approach.

- **Approach 4 (Directed Cycle + Symmetry)**: Also views the letters on a 3-cycle and treats words as paths with “stay” or “move against the arrow” steps, then uses rotational symmetry to collapse the state counts into a single scalar recurrence for total words. Mechanistically this is still a walk on the same finite-state graph with a recurrence relation; the symmetry just simplifies the recurrence. Thus it is the same fundamental method as Approach 1 (state-based recurrence on the transition graph), with an optimization via symmetry.

Hence:
- Cluster 1: Approaches 1 and 4 (finite-state graph / recurrence, with or without symmetry compression).
- Cluster 2: Approach 2 (matrix power / linear algebra).
- Cluster 3: Approach 3 (binary S/D pattern encoding and direct combinatorial count).

problem: A fair coin is flipped $7$ times. What is the probability that at least $5$ consecutive flips come up heads?

response.problem_brief: Find the probability that in 7 fair coin flips there is a run of at least 5 consecutive heads.

approaches.name: Direct Run-Pattern Enumeration
approaches.core_idea: Enumerate all outcome patterns that contain a run of length ≥5 explicitly, classify them by where the run starts and its exact length, and count their configurations without double-counting. Then divide the total favorable count by 2^7.
plan: Define events corresponding to a run of heads of length exactly 5, exactly 6, and exactly 7 within 7 flips
For each run length ℓ (5,6,7), determine all possible starting positions of such a run in a 7-long sequence

For each starting position, specify the constraints on neighboring flips (before and after the run) required so that the longest run is at least that long, and list the possible assignments of tails/heads there

Carefully avoid double-counting sequences that contain runs of different lengths ℓ (e.g., those with a run of 6 also contain a run of 5); use inclusion–exclusion across the pattern classes if necessary
Sum the counts of all valid, distinct sequences that contain at least a length-5 head run
Divide the final count of favorable sequences by 2^7 to get the desired probability
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Counts explicit positional patterns of runs and uses casework/inclusion–exclusion over run lengths and starting positions.

approaches.name: Complement via Recurrence (No Long Run)
approaches.core_idea: Compute the probability of having no run of ≥5 heads in 7 flips via a small finite-state recurrence tracking the current run length of consecutive heads, then subtract from 1. This avoids direct case enumeration of all favorable sequences.
plan: Define states representing the current length of the trailing run of consecutive heads: 0,1,2,3,4 (anything ≥5 would be an absorbing ‘bad’ state)
For each flip, write recurrence relations that update these states when flipping H or T, noting that a tail resets the run length to 0 and a head increases it by 1 (capped at the bad state)

Start from state 0 before any flips and iteratively apply the recurrence for 7 steps, keeping only the probability mass in safe states {0,1,2,3,4} and excluding any transitions that would move into the run ≥5 state
After 7 steps, sum the probabilities of all safe states to obtain P(no run of ≥5 heads in 7 flips)
Compute the desired probability as 1 minus this complement probability
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses a Markov-style run-length state machine and complementary probability via recurrence rather than direct pattern counting.

approaches.name: Manual Enumeration of “Bad” Sequences with Structured Casework
approaches.core_idea: List all sequences without a run of ≥5 heads (the complement) by using structured casework on the maximum run length (0–4) and its placement, then subtract from 1. This is a more combinatorial, non-recursive complement approach.
plan: Classify sequences by their maximum run length of heads: max run = 0,1,2,3,4, ensuring there is no run of length ≥5
For each possible maximum run length r in {0,1,2,3,4}, encode a generic pattern for the arrangement of head-runs and tail-runs whose longest head-block has length r

Within each class, determine how many ways to distribute the total of 7 positions into alternating head and tail blocks consistent with the maximum run constraint, using stars-and-bars style reasoning or small case splitting
Pay attention to boundaries (start/end may be heads or tails) and ensure that no head block exceeds length 4 in any configuration
Sum the counts of sequences for all r to get the total number with no run of ≥5 heads
Divide that by 2^7 to get the complement probability, and subtract from 1 to obtain the required probability
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Counts the complement via combinatorial classification by maximum run length rather than via dynamic recurrence or direct inclusion–exclusion on long runs.

approaches.name: Inclusion–Exclusion Over Starting Positions of Length-5 Runs
approaches.core_idea: Define events A_i where a run of 5 heads starts at position i (i=1..3), and use inclusion–exclusion over these overlapping events, carefully counting extensions to longer runs, to get the total probability of at least one such starting position.
plan: Let A_i be the event that flips i through i+4 are all heads (for i = 1,2,3), which ensures at least a run of 5 starting at i
Compute P(A_i) for a fixed i by counting configurations of the remaining two flips (outside positions i..i+4), and note that all A_i are symmetric
Compute pairwise intersections P(A_i ∩ A_j) for i≠j by analyzing overlapping positions of the 5-head runs (e.g., runs starting at 1 and 2 share 4 positions) and counting consistent sequences
Compute the triple intersection P(A_1 ∩ A_2 ∩ A_3) where all three starting positions contain 5 heads simultaneously, which heavily constrains the entire 7-flip sequence
Apply inclusion–exclusion: P(⋃ A_i) = ΣP(A_i) − ΣP(A_i∩A_j) + P(A_1∩A_2∩A_3) to obtain the probability that there is a 5-head run starting at 1, 2, or 3

Argue that any sequence with at least one run of ≥5 heads must fall into ⋃ A_i in the length-7 setting (i.e., any 5+-run has one of these three starting positions), so this union probability is the required answer
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Frames the problem as a union of ‘5-head run starting here’ events and computes via inclusion–exclusion on their overlaps.

judge_result:
EXPLANATION:
The problem is not “simple” under the given rule: there are several natural ways to count or recurse on runs, so multiple distinct approaches are meaningful.

- **Approach 1 (Direct Run-Pattern Enumeration)** and **Approach 4 (Inclusion–Exclusion Over Starting Positions)** both work by *directly counting favorable sequences that contain a long run*. They operate on the same representational viewpoint: runs of 5+ heads located in the 7-position string, and they both use combinatorial counting on where such runs can start and how they can overlap.
  - Approach 1 organizes by run length (5, 6, 7) and their start positions, and handles overlaps among these pattern classes (possibly via inclusion–exclusion).
  - Approach 4 defines events “5 heads starting at position i” and uses inclusion–exclusion over these starting-position events.
  Despite cosmetic differences (whether you talk about events A_i or pattern classes by length), the core mechanism is the same: **direct combinatorial counting of sequences with a long run, via start positions and overlap corrections**. These belong in one cluster.

- **Approach 2 (Complement via Recurrence)** uses a completely different mechanism: a *finite-state recurrence / Markov-chain style state update* tracking the current run length of heads, and accumulates probability over 7 steps while excluding transitions into a “bad” state. This is a dynamic-programming / recurrence formulation rather than explicit pattern enumeration.

- **Approach 3 (Manual Enumeration of “Bad” Sequences)** is also a complement method, but unlike Approach 2, it is **pure combinatorial enumeration** of sequences with maximum head-run length ≤4, classified by maximum run length and by block decompositions (head-runs and tail-runs). It does not use a state-based recurrence; it uses structural casework and block-counting. This is a distinct mechanism from both the run-start favorable counting (1/4) and the finite-state recurrence (2).

Thus the approaches form three mechanism-level clusters:
1. Direct favorable-set enumeration via run positions and overlaps: Approaches 1 & 4
2. Finite-state recurrence / dynamic programming on run lengths: Approach 2
3. Complement enumeration via block-structure casework: Approach 3

response.problem_brief: Count the real numbers x such that for the given piecewise function f, the composition f(f(x)) equals 5.

approaches.name: Direct Case Unwinding on Inner Argument
approaches.core_idea: First solve f(y)=5 by splitting on the definition of f, then for each solution y find all x such that f(x)=y, again by splitting into f’s two branches. This is the most straightforward composition-unwinding method.
plan: Introduce y = f(x) and rewrite the equation as f(y) = 5
Solve f(y) = 5 by considering the cases y ≥ −4 and y < −4 and get all real y that satisfy it
For each obtained y, solve f(x) = y by again splitting into x ≥ −4 and x < −4
For each branch, solve the corresponding simple equation (quadratic or linear) and impose the relevant inequality condition on x
Collect all distinct x that satisfy at least one branch for some solution y
Count the total number of such x values
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Solves f(f(x)) = 5 by introducing y = f(x) and explicitly solving f(y) = 5, then preimages of each such y under f.

approaches.name: Domain Partitioning on Outer Condition
approaches.core_idea: Partition the x-axis according to which formula is used for both inner and outer f, i.e., whether x and f(x) are each ≥ −4 or < −4, leading to up to four region-cases. On each region, write an explicit non-piecewise expression for f(f(x)) and solve f(f(x)) = 5 with the corresponding inequalities.

Enumerate four logical cases: (x ≥ −4 and f(x) ≥ −4), (x ≥ −4 and f(x) < −4), (x < −4 and f(x) ≥ −4), (x < −4 and f(x) < −4)
For each consistent case, express f(f(x)) explicitly (quadratic plugged into quadratic, quadratic into linear, etc.)
Solve the resulting algebraic equation f(f(x)) = 5 within that case, yielding candidate x’s
Impose the corresponding inequality conditions (for x and f(x)) to discard extraneous roots
Combine all valid x from all consistent cases and count them
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Classifies x by both the inner and outer branch conditions simultaneously, generating up to four explicit formulas for f(f(x)).

approaches.name: Graphical Preimage Counting
approaches.core_idea: Interpret f graphically as a union of a parabola and a line, then consider all points y with f(y)=5 and visually/analytically count how many x map to those y via f. This emphasizes the geometry of the function rather than purely symbolic composition.
plan: Sketch or mentally plot y = f(x): the parabola y = x² − 4 for x ≥ −4 and the line y = x + 3 for x < −4
On the same axes, draw the horizontal line y = 5 and find all intersection points with the graph of f; record their x-coordinates as y-values solving f(y) = 5
For each such y, repeat: draw the horizontal line y = that constant, and find where it intersects the graph of f to determine all x with f(x) = that y
Ensure that each intersection lies on the correct branch (respecting x ≥ −4 or x < −4)
List all distinct x obtained across all such horizontals
Count these x values to obtain the answer
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses the graph of f and intersections with horizontal lines to count preimages iteratively instead of manipulating the algebraic piecewise form first.

approaches.name: Inverse-Function Style Preimage Chaining
approaches.core_idea: Treat each branch of f as a locally invertible function on its natural domain, derive explicit inverses on those domains, and then trace back from the target value 5 through inverse branches while checking domain constraints at each step. This is a structured preimage chain approach.
plan: Identify branches: g(x) = x² − 4 on [−4, ∞) and h(x) = x + 3 on (−∞, −4), and compute their inverses on appropriate ranges (e.g., x = ±√(y+4), x = y − 3)
Solve f(y) = 5 by applying the inverses: find all y such that either g(y)=5 or h(y)=5 while enforcing y in the correct domain of each branch
For each valid y, solve f(x) = y similarly by applying inverses of g and h, again enforcing domain eligibility for x
Systematically list all inverse images: for each y, consider all possible inverse branches that map to it, but only keep those whose outputs lie in the domain of the branch used

This is structurally different from Approach 1: it is based on inverse-branch mappings and range/domain consistency, not just direct solving of \(f(z)=c\) via substitution.

problem: How many even integers between 4000 and 7000 have four different digits?

response.problem_brief: Count even integers from 4000 to 7000 with four distinct digits.

approaches.name: Casework by Thousands Digit and Direct Counting
approaches.core_idea: Separate numbers by their thousands digit (4, 5, or 6), then for each case count possibilities for the units (even), hundreds, and tens digits ensuring distinctness and the range condition. Use careful case distinctions when the last digit interacts with the leading digit.
plan: Split into three main cases: numbers starting with 4, with 5, and with 6, since the thousands digit determines the 4000–7000 range.
In each case, list the allowable choices for the units digit among even digits (0,2,4,6,8) except the thousands digit and respecting distinctness.
For each fixed pair (thousands, units), count permissible hundreds digits among 0–9 excluding the already used two digits.
For each fixed triple (thousands, hundreds, units), count permissible tens digits among 0–9 excluding the already used three digits.
Sum counts over all valid configurations for each thousands-digit case.
Add the results of the three cases to get the total count.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Direct combinatorial counting with explicit casework on the thousands digit and the parity of the units digit.

approaches.name: Complement Counting from All Four-Digit Evens in Range
approaches.core_idea: First count all even integers between 4000 and 7000 (ignoring digit distinctness), then subtract those with at least one repeated digit by counting or bounding the complement. Use structured casework on where the repetition occurs.
plan: Count the total number of even integers from 4000 to 7000 (i.e., 4000–6998 step 2) without digit restrictions.
Classify patterns of repetition (e.g., repeated thousands–hundreds, thousands–tens, thousands–units, internal repeats among hundreds/tens/units).
For each repetition pattern, count how many numbers in 4000–6999 satisfy that pattern while remaining even, using position-wise digit choices with equality constraints.
Use inclusion–exclusion if patterns overlap: sum single-pattern counts and subtract intersections as needed.
Subtract the total number of repeated-digit numbers from the total even numbers to obtain the count with four distinct digits.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Counts all even numbers then removes those with repeated digits using pattern-based complement counting and possible inclusion–exclusion.

approaches.name: Fix Last Digit (Even) First, Then Count Middle Digits
approaches.core_idea: Treat the units digit as primary because of the evenness requirement. For each allowable even units digit, determine the permitted thousands digit (4–6) and then count assignments for hundreds and tens making sure all digits are distinct and within range.
plan: List the five possible even units digits: 0,2,4,6,8.
For each choice of units digit, determine admissible thousands digits among 4,5,6 that do not equal the chosen units digit.
For each fixed (thousands, units) pair, count possible hundreds digits among 0–9 excluding those two digits.
Then for each resulting triple, count tens digits among 0–9 excluding the three already used digits.
Sum over all thousands choices for each fixed units digit, and then sum over all units digits to get the total.
Optionally, handle separately the special subcase when the units digit is 0, since leading-zero issues do not arise but the pool of remaining digits changes slightly.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Starts with the units (even) digit as the primary branching variable, then conditions the thousands digit choices on it before filling middle digits.

approaches.name: Digit Multiset Perspective with Range Filter
approaches.core_idea: View each valid number as an ordered arrangement (permutation) of a 4-element digit set where one element is even and the first element is 4,5, or 6. First select the multiset (actually set) of four distinct digits meeting structural constraints, then count orderings that produce a number in [4000,7000] and are even.
plan: Consider all 4-element subsets of {0,…,9} that contain at least one even digit and at least one of {4,5,6} (for possible thousands digit) and do not contain digits ≥7 as potential thousands digits (since thousands must be 4,5, or 6).
For each such subset, count how many permutations give a 4-digit number with first digit in {4,5,6}, using only digits from the subset and with no leading zero.
Within those permutations, count those with an even units digit (i.e., whose last digit in the permutation is one of the even digits in the subset).
Sum over all qualifying 4-element subsets.
Use symmetry to group subsets into types (e.g., with/without 0, with exactly one of {4,5,6}, etc.) so the counting per type is manageable by hand.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Counts permutations of 4-digit sets satisfying structural digit-set constraints, then filters by first-digit range and even last digit using a multiset/permutation viewpoint.

judge_result:
EXPLANATION:
The problem is combinatorial and supports multiple nontrivial methods, so the simplicity rule does not apply.

- **Approach 1** and **Approach 3** share the same core mechanism: direct positional counting of digits using the multiplication principle with casework. Both:
  - Fix some digit position (thousands in 1, units in 3),
  - Then count allowed choices for the remaining positions under distinctness and evenness,
  - Use straightforward digit-by-digit restrictions.
  The difference is only the order in which positions are fixed; the underlying interpretation and toolset are the same.

- **Approach 2** is conceptually different: it uses **complement counting with inclusion–exclusion**. It first counts all even numbers in the range, then classifies and counts patterns of repeated digits, finally subtracting. This is a different mechanism from direct constructive counting of valid tuples.

- **Approach 4** is also distinct: it views each number as a **permutation of a 4-element digit set**, focusing on choosing digit sets (subsets of {0,…,9}) and then counting permutations satisfying start- and end-digit constraints. That “digit multiset / permutation” perspective differs from both direct place-value casework and complement counting.

Thus we have three unique approaches: direct positional counting, complement with inclusion–exclusion, and digit-set permutation counting.

response.problem_brief: Find the probability that a random 2-step walk on the vertices of a regular octahedron, starting at the top vertex, ends at the bottom vertex.

approaches.name: Direct Vertex-Adjacency Counting
approaches.core_idea: Model the octahedron’s vertices and edges explicitly and count valid paths of length 2 from top to bottom. Use the symmetry of the solid to quickly determine degrees of vertices and possible moves without constructing a full graph-theoretic formalism.
plan: Label the top vertex T, bottom vertex B, and the four equatorial vertices E1–E4.

Determine adjacency: T is connected to all four equatorial vertices; B is also connected to all four equatorial vertices; each equatorial vertex is connected to T, B, and its two adjacent equatorial neighbors (degree 4).
List all possible first moves from T: T → Ei for i=1,…,4 (all equally likely).
For a fixed equatorial vertex Ei, list all its neighbors and identify which of those is B.
Compute the conditional probability that the second move from Ei lands at B (1 out of 4 possibilities).
Use the law of total probability: multiply the probability of reaching each Ei (1/4) by the conditional probability (1/4) and sum, or recognize symmetry and compute once.
Simplify the resulting fraction to get the final probability.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses explicit local degree counting and path enumeration from T through equatorial vertices, exploiting symmetry but without formal Markov chain notation.

approaches.name: Graph-Theoretic Transition Matrix View
approaches.core_idea: View the octahedron as a regular graph and frame the problem as a 2-step transition probability in a Markov chain. Use symmetry and uniform transition probabilities to compute the required entry of the square of the transition matrix conceptually (without actually multiplying matrices numerically).
plan: Represent the octahedron as an undirected graph with vertices {T, B, E1–E4}.
Note that the walk is a Markov chain with transition probability 1/deg(v) from each vertex v to any adjacent vertex.
Identify the degrees: deg(T)=deg(B)=4; each equatorial vertex has degree 4 as well.
Explain that the desired probability is the (T,B) entry of P², where P is the 1-step transition matrix.
Compute conceptually: any 2-step path T → x → B contributes P(T,x)·P(x,B), and only equatorial vertices x can lie on such paths.
For each equatorial vertex Ei, evaluate P(T,Ei)=1/4 and P(Ei,B)=1/4, multiply, and sum over the four equatorial vertices.
Conclude the value of the (T,B) entry of P² and hence the desired probability.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Frames the problem explicitly as computing an entry of the square of a Markov transition matrix, summing over intermediate states.

approaches.name: Combinatorial Path Counting with Total Outcomes
approaches.core_idea: Count the number of length-2 walks starting at the top vertex (total outcomes) and separately count the number of such walks that end at the bottom vertex (favorable outcomes). Then take the ratio, using equidistribution of paths induced by equal step probabilities.
plan: Interpret each walk as an ordered pair of edges (first edge, second edge) starting from T; each distinct path corresponds to a distinct outcome with a fixed probability.
First count total 2-step walks from T: for each possible first neighbor, count how many possible second edges leave that neighbor; sum to get the total number of distinct 2-edge paths.
Then count favorable walks: restrict to those 2-step paths whose final vertex is B; enumerate, via adjacency, all possible intermediate vertices that can lead to B in exactly one more step.
Use symmetry to recognize that each equatorial vertex contributes the same number of favorable 2-step paths T → Ei → B.
Compute the fraction: (number of favorable 2-step paths)/(total number of 2-step paths).
Optionally justify that each 2-step path has equal probability (product of uniform 1/4 steps), so the combinatorial ratio equals the walk probability.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Counts discrete 2-edge paths combinatorially and uses ratio of favorable to total paths, rather than summing conditional probabilities directly.

approaches.name: Conditional Probability via Law of Total Probability on ‘Type’ of Vertex A
approaches.core_idea: Classify the random first-step vertex A into types (equatorial vs. bottom, etc.) and use the law of total probability based on these mutually exclusive cases, then compute the conditional probability of reaching B in the second step from each type. Here, the structure is simple enough that only the equatorial case matters, but the method generalizes.
plan: Partition all possible choices of A by its type: top, bottom, or equatorial; argue from the geometry that only equatorial vertices are reachable in one step from T.
Compute P(A = equatorial vertex Ei) for each i; note that T has four equally likely neighbors so this probability is 1/4 per Ei.
For the case A = Ei, compute P(B is bottom | A = Ei) by examining the 4 neighbors of Ei and counting how many are B.
Write the desired probability as a sum over i: P(B bottom) = Σ P(A=Ei)·P(B bottom | A=Ei).
Use symmetry to simplify: each equatorial vertex contributes the same term, so you can compute once and multiply by 4.
Evaluate and simplify the resulting fraction.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Emphasizes a conditional-probability decomposition over types of the intermediate vertex, presented as a law-of-total-probability case split rather than path counting.

judge_result:
EXPLANATION:
The problem is not so simple that the solution is completely forced; there is room for distinct viewpoints on how to compute the 2-step probability.

- **Approach 1 (Direct Vertex-Adjacency Counting)** and **Approach 4 (Conditional Probability / Law of Total Probability)** use the same core mechanism:
  - Both condition on the intermediate vertex \(A\), which must be one of the equatorial vertices.
  - Both use adjacency information at \(A\) to find \(P(\text{second step hits bottom} \mid A)\).
  - Both then sum over the equatorial vertices (explicitly invoking or effectively using the law of total probability).
  These are the same conceptual interpretation: straightforward conditional probability based on the intermediate vertex.

- **Approach 2 (Graph-Theoretic Transition Matrix View)** uses a different mechanism:
  - Frames the situation explicitly as a Markov chain on a regular graph.
  - Interprets the desired probability as an entry of \(P^2\), the square of the transition matrix.
  - Though it still decomposes via intermediate states, its language and conceptual framing is matrix/Markov-chain based rather than basic conditional probability on vertices.

- **Approach 3 (Combinatorial Path Counting)** is yet another different mechanism:
  - Counts total 2-step walks as combinatorial objects (ordered pairs of edges).
  - Separately counts favorable 2-step walks ending at the bottom.
  - Uses symmetry/uniformity to justify that probability is (favorable paths)/(total paths).
  This is a counting approach rather than a conditioning-on-intermediate-vertex probability computation.

Thus we have three distinct underlying approaches:
1. Conditioning on intermediate vertex / law of total probability (Approaches 1 & 4).
2. Markov chain / transition matrix viewpoint (Approach 2).
3. Combinatorial path counting viewpoint (Approach 3).

response.problem_brief: Find the area of triangle ACE formed from two right triangles ABC and ABD sharing side AB, where AB=6, AC=10, BD=6, and E is a specific interior point on segment CD as defined in the diagram.

approaches.name: Coordinate Geometry with Vector Definition of E
approaches.core_idea: Place the figure on a coordinate plane using the natural right-angle orientation, express all vertices as coordinates, determine point E from its given vector (affine) combination of A and D, then compute triangle ACE’s area via a coordinate-area formula.
plan: Place A at (0,0), B at (6,0), C at (0,10), D at (6,6) using the right angles and side lengths.
Translate the given Asymptote description of E, e.g., E = (6*A + 10*D)/16, into a coordinate expression for E.
Compute the explicit coordinates of E from A and D.
Use a standard coordinate area formula for triangle ACE, such as the determinant/cross-product formula or the shoelace formula.
Simplify the resulting expression to obtain the numeric area of triangle ACE.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses explicit Cartesian coordinates and the vector/affine definition of E directly from the code, then a standard determinant/shoelace area formula.

approaches.name: Barycentric/Section-Ratio Interpretation on Segment AD
approaches.core_idea: View E as a point dividing segment AD in a fixed ratio derived from its affine combination, then express vectors for AE and CE and compute the area via vector cross products or base–height relationships without writing full coordinates for all points.
plan: Interpret E’s definition (6*A + 10*D)/16 as giving a specific ratio AE:ED on segment AD.
Express CE as a linear combination of CA and CD using the known geometry of the two right triangles.
Use vector relations (e.g., let AC and AB be basis vectors) and represent AE and CE in this basis using the section ratio and triangle side data.
Compute the area of triangle ACE as half the magnitude of the cross product of AE and CE expressed in that basis.
Simplify symbolically using the known lengths and perpendicularity of AC and AB to get the numeric area.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Treats E via its internal division ratio on AD and works in an abstract vector/basis framework rather than assigning full numeric coordinates to all points.

approaches.name: Area Decomposition in Quadrilateral ACBD
approaches.core_idea: Compute the total area of a larger polygon (such as ACBD) from simple right triangles, then express the area of triangle ACE as a sum/difference of areas of smaller triangles whose bases or heights are easy to relate by similarity or proportionality.
plan: Identify the convex polygon ACBD, whose area can be expressed as the sum/difference of areas of the two right triangles ABC and ABD.
Write the area of triangle ACE in terms of areas of triangles within ACBD, such as ABC, ABD, ABE, CBE, or ADE, depending on where E lies on segment CD.
Use the linearity of area with respect to points on a segment: for a point E dividing CD in a fixed ratio, areas of triangles with the same altitude but different bases scale in the same ratio.
Relate the area of triangle ACE to the area of a known triangle like ACD using the ratio in which E divides CD.

Compute the needed ratio from the definition of E (using only segment lengths and parallel/perpendicular relations), and then apply it to get the area of triangle ACE from the area of ACD (and possibly subtract/add other sub-areas if necessary).
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Finds the desired area purely by comparing and scaling areas of sub-triangles in the composite quadrilateral, avoiding explicit vector or coordinate formulas.

approaches.name: Similarity-Based Height Ratio Method
approaches.core_idea: Use the right angles and shared sides to identify similar triangles that relate various altitudes to base lines, then express the altitude of triangle ACE (from C or E to base AE or AC) in terms of known lengths via those similarities, and compute its area via ½·base·height.
plan: Determine which segments are parallel or form right angles (e.g., AB ⟂ AC and AB ⟂ BD, so AC ∥ BD) to locate similar triangles involving C, D, and E.
Locate E on CD using its definition so that ratios like CE:ED or AE:AD can be expressed using similar triangles and proportional segments.

Choose a convenient base for triangle ACE, such as AC, and aim to express the perpendicular distance from E to AC using similarity relations among right triangles formed by dropping suitable altitudes.
Write the area of triangle ACE as ½·AC·(distance from E to AC).
Replace that distance using the similarity-based ratios derived from the configuration and the given side lengths.
Simplify the expression to obtain the numeric area.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Relies on constructing and exploiting similar right triangles to obtain a needed height ratio, then uses ½·base·height rather than coordinate determinants or direct area scaling.

judge_result:
EXPLANATION:
The problem is not “simple” in the sense of the simplicity rule: there is enough structure (two right triangles, a special point defined affinely, internal triangle area) to support genuinely different methods.

- **Approach 1 (Coordinate geometry)** and **Approach 2 (Barycentric/vector)** both use essentially the same *analytic vector/coordinate mechanism*: represent points as linear combinations in a 2D vector space, determine the position of \(E\) via its affine combination, and compute the area using a determinant/cross-product formula.  
  - Approach 1 does this concretely with explicit Cartesian coordinates.  
  - Approach 2 does this more abstractly using vectors and section ratios, but still ends with area as \(\frac12 \|\vec{AE}\times\vec{CE}\|\).  
  Despite stylistic differences (explicit coordinates vs. abstract basis), the underlying mathematical toolset and interpretation are the same: linear algebra/coordinate geometry with cross-product area.

- **Approach 3 (Area decomposition in \(ACBD\))** is different. It treats the figure synthetically via **area additivity and linearity**: viewing \(E\) as dividing a segment in a ratio, then expressing \([ACE]\) as a sum/difference or scaled portion of areas of other triangles within the quadrilateral, invoking the fact that areas scale linearly with segment division when sharing an altitude. This is an area-ratio/decomposition viewpoint rather than an explicit coordinate/vector computation.

- **Approach 4 (Similarity-based height ratio)** is also synthetic but conceptually different from Approach 3. It focuses on **similar triangles and altitudes**: use right angles and parallels to find similar triangles, extract ratios to compute a specific perpendicular distance (height) from \(E\) to a chosen base, then use \( \tfrac12 \cdot \text{base} \cdot \text{height} \). There is no area decomposition into subtriangles as the primary engine; the key mechanism is similarity-implied length ratios to get a height.

Thus, the approaches naturally cluster into three mechanism-level groups:
1. Analytic vector/coordinate (Approaches 1 and 2),
2. Synthetic area decomposition/linearity (Approach 3),
3. Synthetic similarity-altitude method (Approach 4).

- **Approach 1 (Coordinate geometry)** and **Approach 2 (Barycentric/vector)** both use essentially the same *analytic vector/coordinate mechanism*: represent points as linear combinations in a 2D vector space, determine the position of \(E\) via its affine combination, and compute the area using a determinant/cross-product formula.  
  - Approach 1 does this concretely with explicit Cartesian coordinates.  
  - Approach 2 does this more abstractly using vectors and section ratios, but still ends with area as \(\frac12 \|\vec{AE}\times\vec{CE}\|\).  
  Despite stylistic differences (explicit coordinates vs. abstract basis), the underlying mathematical toolset and interpretation are the same: linear algebra/coordinate geometry with cross-product area.

- **Approach 3 (Area decomposition in \(ACBD\))** is different. It treats the figure synthetically via **area additivity and linearity**: viewing \(E\) as dividing a segment in a ratio, then expressing \([ACE]\) as a sum/difference or scaled portion of areas of other triangles within the quadrilateral, invoking the fact that areas scale linearly with segment division when sharing an altitude. This is an area-ratio/decomposition viewpoint rather than an explicit coordinate/vector computation.

- **Approach 4 (Similarity-based height ratio)** is also synthetic but conceptually different from Approach 3. It focuses on **similar triangles and altitudes**: use right angles and parallels to find similar triangles, extract ratios to compute a specific perpendicular distance (height) from \(E\) to a chosen base, then use \( \tfrac12 \cdot \text{base} \cdot \text{height} \). There is no area decomposition into subtriangles as the primary engine; the key mechanism is similarity-implied length ratios to get a height.

Thus, the approaches naturally cluster into three mechanism-level groups:
1. Analytic vector/coordinate (Approaches 1 and 2),
2. Synthetic area decomposition/linearity (Approach 3),
3. Synthetic similarity-altitude method (Approach 4).

problem:
Suppose that we have an equation $y=ax^2+bx+c$ whose graph is a parabola with vertex $(3,2)$, vertical axis of symmetry, and contains the point $(1,0)$.

What is $(a, b, c)$?

response.problem_brief: Find the coefficients (a,b,c) of a quadratic with given vertex and a point on its graph.

approaches.name: Vertex Form then Expand
approaches.core_idea: Use the fact that a parabola with a vertical axis and vertex (h,k) can be written in vertex form y = a(x−h)² + k. Plug in the known point to solve for a, then expand to standard form to read off a, b, c.
plan: Write the quadratic in vertex form as y = A(x − 3)² + 2, where A is unknown.
Substitute the point (1,0) into this equation to get an equation in A.
Solve that equation to find the value of A.
Expand A(x − 3)² + 2 into the form ax² + bx + c by algebraic expansion.
Identify a, b, and c from the expanded expression.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses the vertex form of a parabola directly, then expands.

approaches.name: System from General Form and Vertex Conditions
approaches.core_idea: Start from the general form y = ax² + bx + c and impose the conditions for a vertex at (3,2): vanishing derivative at x=3 and y(3)=2, plus y(1)=0. Solve the resulting system for a, b, c.
plan: Write y = ax² + bx + c as the general quadratic.
Compute the derivative y' = 2ax + b, and set y'(3) = 0 to enforce the vertex at x = 3, giving one equation in a and b.
Set y(3) = 2 to use that the vertex lies on the graph, giving a second equation in a, b, c.
Set y(1) = 0 to use the given point (1,0), giving a third equation in a, b, c.
Solve the resulting linear system of three equations in a, b, c.
Read off the values of a, b, and c.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses calculus (derivative zero at vertex) plus point conditions to form a linear system.

approaches.name: Axis of Symmetry and Symmetric Point
approaches.core_idea: Use the vertical axis of symmetry x=3 and the point (1,0) to infer that (5,0) is also on the parabola. Then fit a quadratic through three known points (1,0), (3,2), and (5,0).
plan: Note that the axis of symmetry is x = 3, and (1,0) is 2 units left of the axis.
Conclude by symmetry that (5,0), which is 2 units right of x = 3, is also on the parabola.
Write the general form y = ax² + bx + c.
Plug in the three points (1,0), (3,2), and (5,0) to obtain three equations in a, b, c.
Solve this 3×3 system for a, b, and c by substitution or elimination.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Exploits geometric symmetry to generate a third point before solving a three-point interpolation system.

approaches.name: Horizontal Shift of a Standard Parabola
approaches.core_idea: Model the parabola as a vertical shift of a horizontally shifted standard parabola y = A(x−3)², then use the vertex’s y-coordinate as an additional parameter. Determine both A and the vertical shift using the given point, then expand to find a, b, c.
plan: Start with the generic form of a vertically scaled, horizontally shifted parabola y = A(x − 3)² + k, treating both A and k as unknowns.
Use the fact that the vertex is at (3,2) to set y(3) = k = 2, thereby determining k immediately.
Substitute k = 2 into y = A(x − 3)² + 2.
Plug the given point (1,0) into this equation to solve for A.
Once A is found, rewrite y in standard form by expanding A(x − 3)² + 2 into ax² + bx + c.
Read off a, b, and c from the resulting expression.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Treats both the vertical scale and vertical shift as parameters in a shifted-vertex template before fixing them via vertex and point conditions.

judge_result:
EXPLANATION:
The problem is not “simple” in the sense of being forced into a single mechanical method; several conceptually different ways to encode the vertex/axis information are possible.

- **Approach 1** and **Approach 4** use the same core mechanism:  
  They both write the quadratic directly in **vertex form** \(y = A(x-3)^2 + k\), use the vertex \((3,2)\) to fix \(k=2\), then use the point \((1,0)\) to determine \(A\), and finally expand to standard form. The slight difference in the order of parameter introduction does not change the underlying method.

- **Approach 2** uses a different mechanism:  
  It starts from **general form** \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\), then uses **calculus/derivative conditions** for a vertex: \(y'(3)=0\) and \(y(3)=2\), plus \(y(1)=0\), giving a linear system in \(a,b,c\).

- **Approach 3** uses yet another mechanism:  
  It exploits **geometric symmetry** about the axis \(x=3\) to infer a second point \((5,0)\), then fits a quadratic through three points \((1,0), (3,2), (5,0)\) via a 3×3 linear system.

Thus there are three distinct underlying approaches.

problem: The expression $x^2 + 13x + 30$ can be written as  $(x + a)(x + b),$ and the expression $x^2 + 5x - 50$ written as $(x + b)(x - c)$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are integers. What is the value of $a + b + c$?

response.problem_brief: Find integers a, b, c such that x^2+13x+30=(x+a)(x+b) and x^2+5x−50=(x+b)(x−c), then compute a+b+c.

approaches.name: Direct coefficient comparison
approaches.core_idea: Expand the factored forms and equate coefficients with the given quadratics. This yields a small system of equations in a, b, c that can be solved algebraically.
plan: Write (x+a)(x+b)=x^2+(a+b)x+ab and equate to x^2+13x+30 to get a+b=13 and ab=30.
Write (x+b)(x−c)=x^2+(b−c)x−bc and equate to x^2+5x−50 to get b−c=5 and −bc=−50, i.e., bc=50.
Use a+b=13 and ab=30 to find the integer pair (a,b) among factor pairs of 30 whose sum is 13.
Use bc=50 and b−c=5 to find integers (b,c) among factor pairs of 50 whose difference is 5.
Check that the b obtained from both systems is consistent; this pins down a, b, c uniquely.
Compute a+b+c from the found values.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Solves entirely via comparing coefficients of expanded products to form and solve a small system of Diophantine equations.

approaches.name: Root-based matching of factorizations
approaches.core_idea: Interpret a, b, c in terms of the roots of the quadratics. Both factorizations share the linear factor x+b, so their common root gives b directly, then deduce a and c from the other roots.
plan: Note that x^2+13x+30=(x+a)(x+b) has roots −a and −b, and x^2+5x−50=(x+b)(x−c) has roots −b and c.
Use the quadratic formula or standard factoring to find the two roots of x^2+13x+30; assign them to −a and −b.
Similarly, factor x^2+5x−50 to find its two roots; assign them to −b and c.
Identify the common root between the two quadratics; set that equal to −b and thereby determine b.
Once b is known, read off a as the negative of the other root of the first quadratic and c as the other root of the second quadratic.
Compute a+b+c.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses the shared root implied by the common factor (x+b) and explicit root-finding rather than coefficient equations on a, b, c.

approaches.name: Factor by integer pair search for each quadratic
approaches.core_idea: Independently factor each quadratic by seeking integer pairs for the constant term with the correct sum for the linear coefficient, then reconcile the factorizations using the shared factor (x+b).
plan: For x^2+13x+30, list integer factor pairs of 30 and find the pair (p,q) whose sum is 13 so that x^2+13x+30=(x+p)(x+q).
For x^2+5x−50, list integer factor pairs of −50 and find the pair (r,s) whose sum is 5 so that x^2+5x−50=(x+r)(x+s).
Compare the two factorizations (x+p)(x+q) and (x+r)(x+s) with the desired forms (x+a)(x+b) and (x+b)(x−c).
Identify which factor among (x+p),(x+q) and among (x+r),(x+s) must match x+b; equate that coefficient to determine b.
Once b is chosen, set the remaining first quadratic factor as x+a to find a, and express the remaining second quadratic factor as x−c to find c.
Compute a+b+c.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Relies on classic trial-and-error integer factoring of each quadratic and then matches factors structurally, instead of solving equations in a, b, c.

approaches.name: Eliminate b via symmetric relations
approaches.core_idea: Use the sum and product relations from each factorization to express a and c directly in terms of b, then combine these with cross-relations (like comparing sums of all three parameters) to eliminate b without fully solving each subsystem first.
plan: From (x+a)(x+b)=x^2+13x+30 obtain a+b=13 and ab=30; express a=13−b and substitute into ab=30 to get a quadratic equation in b.
From (x+b)(x−c)=x^2+5x−50 obtain b−c=5 and bc=50; express c=b−5 and substitute into bc=50 to get another quadratic equation in b.
Simplify both resulting quadratic equations in b and observe they must have a common integer solution for b.
Compare the two polynomials in b (e.g., subtract one from the other) to reduce to a simpler linear condition that b must satisfy.
Solve this simpler condition to find the viable integer b, then back-substitute into a=13−b and c=b−5.
Add a+b+c.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Treats the two coefficient systems as equations in b alone and uses elimination/comparison of the resulting quadratics to isolate b, rather than directly searching factor pairs or using roots.

judge_result:
EXPLANATION:
The problem is not in the “simple/forced” category, since there are several natural ways to use the given factorizations and parameter relations.

- **Approach 1 (Direct coefficient comparison)** and **Approach 3 (Factor by integer pair search)** share the same core mechanism:
  - Both use the identities \((x+a)(x+b) = x^2 + (a+b)x + ab\) and \((x+b)(x-c) = x^2 + (b-c)x - bc\), i.e., sum and product of the “shift” parameters matching the quadratic’s coefficients.
  - They then use these sum/product conditions to pin down integer values (either via explicit equations, as in Approach 1, or via systematic factor-pair search, as in Approach 3).
  - Conceptually, both are coefficient-based factorization using integer factor pairs; the difference is only stylistic (equations vs. a table of factor pairs), not a distinct mathematical viewpoint.

- **Approach 2 (Root-based matching of factorizations)** uses a different interpretation:
  - It views \(-a, -b, c\) as *roots* of the quadratics and explicitly finds the roots (possibly with the quadratic formula or factoring), then matches the common root to identify \(b\).
  - The reasoning is framed in terms of solving equations for roots and matching shared zeros, rather than equating coefficients or searching factor pairs directly.
  - This root-focused viewpoint is a distinct representational framework from the coefficient-sum/product approach of 1 and 3.

- **Approach 4 (Eliminate b via symmetric relations)** also differs:
  - It starts from the same coefficient relations but treats them as a system in \(a,b,c\); expresses \(a\) and \(c\) in terms of \(b\), forms two equations in \(b\), and uses algebraic elimination/comparison of polynomials in \(b\) to find a common solution.
  - The central mechanism is elimination in a small algebraic system, rather than factoring each quadratic independently or working with roots.
  - This is a more “system-of-equations/symmetric relations” perspective, distinct from both the pure factoring (1,3) and the root matching (2).

Thus the approaches group as:
- Group 1 (same core mechanism): Approaches 1 and 3.
- Group 2: Approach 2.
- Group 3: Approach 4.

problem: A card is chosen at random from a standard deck of 52 cards, and then it is replaced and another card is chosen. What is the probability that at least one of the cards is a diamond or an ace?

response.problem_brief: Find the probability that, in two draws with replacement from a 52-card deck, at least one card is a diamond or an ace.

approaches.name: Complement Rule with Union Counting
approaches.core_idea: Count how many cards are diamonds or aces, then use the complement rule for "at least one" over two independent draws. This uses basic set counting and independence.
plan: Count the number of diamonds in the deck (13).
Count the number of aces (4) and subtract the overlap (ace of diamonds) to avoid double counting, giving |diamonds ∪ aces|.
Compute the probability p of getting a diamond or ace in a single draw using that count over 52.
Use independence to find the probability that neither draw is a diamond or ace: (1 − p)^2.
Apply the complement rule: probability(at least one) = 1 − (probability of none).
Optionally simplify the resulting fraction.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses set union counting once, then complements over two draws, leveraging independence.

approaches.name: Direct Inclusion–Exclusion Over Outcomes
approaches.core_idea: Work directly on the two-draw sample space and apply inclusion–exclusion on the events that each draw is a diamond-or-ace. This treats each draw as a separate event and computes union of events across draws.
plan: Define event A: first draw is a diamond or ace; event B: second draw is a diamond or ace.
Compute P(A) and P(B) individually by finding the single-draw probability of diamond or ace (same for both).
Because of replacement, use independence to compute P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B).
Apply inclusion–exclusion: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
Express everything in terms of the single-draw probability and simplify.
Optionally cross-check that this matches the complement approach.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Treats the two draws as separate events and uses inclusion–exclusion at the level of the two-draw probability space.

approaches.name: Complement via Direct Counting of Ordered Pairs
approaches.core_idea: Enumerate favorable/unfavorable ordered pairs in the 52×52 sample space by direct counting, then use the complement for "at least one" in terms of exact pair counts.
plan: Note that the sample space has 52·52 ordered pairs (first draw, second draw).
Count the number of cards that are neither diamonds nor aces in a single draw by subtracting the diamond-or-ace count from 52.
Compute the number of ordered pairs where both cards are neither diamonds nor aces as (non-special-count)^2.
Use the complement in the sample space: favorable pairs = total pairs − pairs with no diamonds or aces.
Divide the favorable count by 52·52 to get the desired probability.
Simplify the ratio if needed.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Counts ordered pairs explicitly in the 52×52 sample space rather than working with per-draw probabilities first.

approaches.name: Casework on Exact Number of Special Cards (0,1,2)
approaches.core_idea: Do a full partition into disjoint cases based on how many of the two draws are diamonds-or-aces, then sum the probabilities of the 1 and 2 cases. This emphasizes disjoint casework rather than complements or inclusion–exclusion.
plan: Let p be the single-draw probability of a diamond or ace, found via counting such cards over 52.
Compute the probability of exactly 0 such cards in two draws: (1 − p)^2.
Compute the probability of exactly 1 such card: choose which draw (2 ways), then multiply p·(1 − p).
Compute the probability of exactly 2 such cards: p^2.
Sum the probabilities of the 1-card and 2-card cases to get the final probability.
Optionally verify that the sum equals 1 − (1 − p)^2 as a check.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses a full partition into exact-count cases (0,1,2 special cards) and sums the desired disjoint probabilities, rather than using a single complement or two-event union formula.

judge_result:
EXPLANATION:
The problem is not “simple” in the sense of forcing a single mechanical method; it naturally allows several standard probability viewpoints (complement, union of events across draws, full case partitioning), so the simplicity rule does not apply.

Grouping by core mechanism:

- **Approach 1 (Complement Rule with Union Counting)**  
  Uses: compute single-draw probability of “diamond or ace,” then use **complement of ‘none in two draws’** via independence: \(1 - (1-p)^2\).  
  Core mechanism: complement of “no success” using single-event probability.

- **Approach 3 (Complement via Direct Counting of Ordered Pairs)**  
  Uses: explicit \(52 \times 52\) sample space and counts ordered pairs with no special cards, then complements. This is the *same core mechanism* as Approach 1: probability of at least one = 1 − probability of none. The only difference is representational (single-draw probability vs full sample space), not a different conceptual tool.

  ⇒ Approaches 1 and 3 form **one cluster**: “complement of zero successes.”

- **Approach 2 (Direct Inclusion–Exclusion Over Outcomes)**  
  Defines events A and B for each draw, computes \(P(A\cup B)\) via **inclusion–exclusion on the union across time steps**: \(P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\).  
  Though algebraically equivalent to the complement formula, the mechanism is conceptually “union of events across draws with inclusion–exclusion,” not “count none and complement.”

  ⇒ This is a **second, distinct cluster**.

- **Approach 4 (Casework on Exact Number of Special Cards (0,1,2))**  
  Partitions into disjoint cases by **exact count of special cards (0, 1, 2)** in two independent draws and sums probabilities of the 1 and 2 cases. This is a binomial-style case partition rather than union or complement reasoning, even though it simplifies to the same expression.

  ⇒ This is a **third, distinct cluster**.

Thus there are three fundamentally different mechanisms: complement-of-none, inclusion–exclusion on time-indexed events, and full count-based casework on the number of successes.

problem: How many different four-letter arrangements can be formed using the six letters $A, B, C, D, E$ and $F$, if the first letter must be $C$, one of the other letters must be $B$, and no letter can be used more than once in the arrangement?

response.problem_brief: Count 4-letter arrangements from {A,B,C,D,E,F} with first letter fixed as C, exactly one of remaining positions must contain B, and no repetitions allowed.

approaches.name: Direct positional counting
approaches.core_idea: Fix C in the first position, then choose which of the remaining three positions hosts B, and finally fill the leftover two positions with any distinct letters from the remaining pool. Multiply the counts for each independent choice. This is a straightforward rule-of-product argument.
plan: Fix the first position as C (no choice).
Choose one of the 3 remaining positions to place B.
From the remaining 4 letters {A,D,E,F}, choose 2 distinct letters to occupy the remaining 2 positions.
Count the number of ways to choose these 2 letters (order matters, since positions are distinct).
Multiply: (choices for B’s position) × (arrangements of the 2 other letters).
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses the multiplication principle with an explicit choice of B’s position among the remaining slots, then permutes the remaining letters.

approaches.name: Permutation formula viewpoint
approaches.core_idea: Interpret the problem as a restricted permutation of a 4-element subset: C and B must be included, and the first position is fixed to C while B must be in one of the last three. Count permutations of chosen letters, then enforce the positional constraints using factorial-based reasoning.
plan: Note that each valid arrangement is a permutation of a 4-letter subset that must include C and B plus 2 letters from {A,D,E,F}.
Choose the additional 2 letters from the 4 available non-C,B letters using combinations (order not yet considered).
For each chosen 4-letter set, count permutations where C is first.
Among those permutations with C first, count those where B is not in first position (i.e., B can appear in any of the remaining positions).
Use factorial expressions (e.g., (4−1)!) to get the number of acceptable permutations per chosen 4-letter subset.
Multiply by the number of ways to choose the 2 extra letters.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Starts from selecting 4-letter subsets including C and B, then uses factorial/permutation counts with C fixed in first position.

approaches.name: Complementary counting on B’s placement
approaches.core_idea: View the total permutations with first letter C and then subtract those where the constraint involving B fails. Specifically, count all 4-letter arrangements starting with C (with no further restriction), then subtract arrangements where B does not appear at all or where B appears in an invalid position if that were relevant.
plan: Count all 4-letter arrangements from the 6 letters with first letter fixed as C (no restriction on B).
From these, subtract arrangements where B is not used among the remaining 3 positions (i.e., all 3 letters are from {A,D,E,F}).
Note that because C is already placed, B cannot be in first position; thus any arrangement that includes B automatically satisfies “one of the other letters is B.”
Compute: (total with first C) − (those with no B).
Obtain the desired count as this difference.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Counts all permutations with first C and removes those omitting B entirely, exploiting that B cannot occupy the first fixed position.

approaches.name: Casework on the position of B
approaches.core_idea: Partition the problem into disjoint cases based on the exact position of B (2nd, 3rd, or 4th). For each case, fill the remaining two positions from the allowed letters and sum the results. This is an explicit case-by-case application of the addition principle.
plan: Fix C in the first position.
Consider three separate cases: (i) B in position 2, (ii) B in position 3, (iii) B in position 4.
For each case, identify the two remaining empty positions and the available letters {A,D,E,F}.
Count the permutations of 2 distinct letters from {A,D,E,F} into those two positions (order matters).
Compute this count for one case, note it is the same for each of the three symmetric cases.
Multiply the per-case count by 3 (for the three possible B-positions) and sum to get the total.
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses explicit disjoint casework on B’s exact position rather than treating its position as a single combinatorial choice.

judge_result:
EXPLANATION:
The problem is not in the “simple/forced” category; it supports several standard counting strategies.

- **Approach 1 (Direct positional counting)** and **Approach 4 (Casework on the position of B)** use the same underlying mechanism:
  - Both fix C in the first position.
  - Both then determine where B goes among the remaining three positions.

problem: Four packages are delivered to four houses, one to each house. If these packages are randomly delivered, what is the probability that exactly two of them are delivered to the correct houses? Express your answer as a common fraction.

response.problem_brief: Find the probability that, when 4 distinct packages are randomly delivered to 4 distinct houses, exactly two are delivered to the correct houses.

approaches.name: Direct Counting with Derangements of 2 Items
approaches.core_idea: Treat the event "exactly two correct" by choosing which two are correct and forcing the remaining two to be wrong. Then use derangement ideas on the remaining sub-permutation (of size 2) to count valid outcomes and divide by total permutations.
plan: Compute the total number of ways to deliver 4 distinct packages to 4 distinct houses as 4!
Choose which 2 of the 4 packages are correctly delivered using a binomial coefficient
Fix those two chosen packages to their correct houses
Consider the remaining 2 packages and houses and count the permutations in which neither of these remaining packages goes to its correct house (derangements of 2 elements)
Multiply the choice count by the number of derangements of the remaining 2 to get the favorable outcomes
Divide the favorable count by 4! and simplify the resulting fraction
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses combination choice for the correct packages plus explicit derangement count on the remaining 2.

approaches.name: Systematic Case Analysis on Positions
approaches.core_idea: View the arrangement positionally: enforce correctness on two specified positions and then directly list or argue the possible misplacements of the other two packages to ensure they are both incorrect, without invoking the derangement formula by name.
plan: Label packages and houses with matching numbers 1–4 to define what "correct" means
Choose two specific positions (houses) to be correct and fix their packages there
Write out the two remaining packages and two remaining houses in a small 2×2 table
Enumerate all permutations of these two remaining packages over the two remaining houses
From this enumeration, count how many permutations have both of these remaining packages incorrect
Generalize this count to all possible choices of which two houses are correct (using a combinatorial factor)
Divide the total number of favorable permutations by 4! to get the probability
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Counts incorrect placements for the remaining two packages via explicit small-case enumeration rather than derangement reasoning.

approaches.name: Inclusion–Exclusion on "Correct" Indicators
approaches.core_idea: Use inclusion–exclusion on events that specific packages are correctly delivered to count permutations with exactly two correct locations by first counting those with at least two correct, then subtracting those with three or four correct.
plan: Define events A_i: package i is delivered to the correct house, for i = 1,…,4
Compute the number of permutations with a given set of k specified A_i all true by fixing those k positions and permuting the remaining 4−k freely
Use inclusion–exclusion to find the number of permutations with at least 2 correct houses: sum over all |A_i∩A_j|, subtract sums over |A_i∩A_j∩A_k|, add back |A_1∩A_2∩A_3∩A_4|
Separately compute the number of permutations with at least 3 correct houses using the same type of inclusion–exclusion restricted to k≥3
Obtain the number with exactly 2 correct as (at least 2 correct) minus (at least 3 correct)
Divide that exact count by 4! to obtain the probability
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Uses inclusion–exclusion on events of individual packages being correct to isolate the count of exactly two correct deliveries.

approaches.name: Probability via Sequential Conditioning
approaches.core_idea: Imagine delivering packages one by one and condition on which two will be correct, translating the combinatorics into a probability tree that encodes the same counts via conditional probabilities at each step.
plan: Label the houses 1–4 and consider delivering packages in a fixed order (e.g., by house number)
Choose which two houses will end up with the correct packages using a combinatorial factor in the probability expression
Condition on delivering the correct package when you reach a house designated to be correct and delivering an incorrect package when you reach a house designated to be incorrect
For the two "correct" houses, compute the product of conditional probabilities that the correct package is available at that time and chosen
For the two "incorrect" houses, compute the product of conditional probabilities that the current house does not receive its own package (given remaining packages)
Multiply these conditional probabilities together, then multiply by the number of ways to choose the pair of correct houses
Sum or simplify to obtain the overall probability of exactly two correct deliveries
approaches.uniqueness_signature: Derives the probability via a stepwise probability tree/conditioning argument instead of pure counting formulas.
